paragraphs: (1) In the Mishnah: Maaser Sheni 5:15; Sotah 9:10; Parah 3:5.

(2) His son was Mattityahu, as mentioned in the prayers: ‘Mattityahu son of Yochanan the high priest, the Hasmonean.’ This means Yochanan, who was called the Hasmonean and was Mattityahu’s father. So too Yesod Olam, and in Megillah, chapter 1: ‘Shimon the Righteous and Mattityahu son of Yochanan the high priest, the Hasmonean, and his sons, who stood for Israel in the Greeks’ days.’ Maimonides writes in chapter 6 of the name-identification section of his Introduction to the Mishnah: ‘Yochanan the high priest, son of Mattityahu.’ Halikhot Olam likewise writes: ‘Yochanan the high priest, son of Mattityahu, who lived in the Hasmoneans’ days.’ These are its words, page 3a, end: ‘First generation: Shimon the Righteous. Second generation: Antigonos and Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom. Third generation: Yose ben Yoezer and Yose ben Yochanan. Fourth generation: Yochanan ben Mattityahu, Yehoshua ben Perachyah, and Nittai of Arbel.’ End quotation. Yuchasin, in Raavad’s tradition of transmission, likewise cites in a gloss Maimonides’ introduction to Zeraim. But they are mistaken, for Yochanan the high priest was Mattityahu’s father. In the chapter Yesh Nochalin it appears that he and his son lived in Yannai’s days, when they consecrated his property; this is puzzling. He received from Antigonos in the year 3500, ninety-two years after the Temple’s construction (Yuchasin, sequence of generations). Zayit Raanan, beginning of Chukkat, writes: Rabbi Shimshon, Parah, chapter 3, mishnah 5, wrote that he lived in Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai’s days. In Berakhot 29a Abaye said that he was Yannai, who killed the sages and lived in Rabbi Shimon ben Shetach’s days. He preceded Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai by much, for the latter lived at the destruction, while Shimon ben Shetach preceded Shemayah and Avtalyon. End quotation. That is, Shemayah and Avtalyon were Hillel’s teachers, and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was Hillel’s student.

(3) He was righteous and instituted many enactments. He enacted the demai regulations and abolished the declaration concerning the second tithe (end of Maaser Sheni). He abolished the sound of the hammer in Jerusalem during the intermediate festival days. The commentators did not cite this, because it seemed to them that this is permitted when one has nothing to eat, as related in Moed Katan; see Sotah 47. He prepared two red cows, as related in Parah 3:5. He also abolished the awakeners, who used to say ‘Awake! Why do You sleep?’ He abolished the strikers, arranging rings by which to bring the oxen to the ground to slaughter them for offerings. In Sotah 33, when he came out of the Holy of Holies, he heard a heavenly voice: ‘The young men have prevailed,’ and so forth; so too Shir HaShirim Rabbah. In Pesachim 57a: ‘The Temple court cries out again: “Raise your heads, gates, and let Yochanan ben Narbai, Pankai’s student, enter and fill his belly with Heaven’s sacred offerings,”’ and so forth. Chiddushei Aggadot writes: one should examine why he is counted here among the worthy priests, while Yoma 9a lists the righteous men of the Second Temple who lasted many years—Shimon the Righteous, forty years; Yochanan the high priest, eighty years; Yishmael ben Pabi, ten years; some say the eleven years of Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom—but does not count Yochanan ben Narbai. Perhaps Yochanan the high priest and Yochanan ben Narbai are one and the same. This can resolve the following point. That is, according to our interpretation, Yochanan ben Narbai would be Yochanan who served eighty years and became a Sadducee. Concerning Yishmael ben Pabi, it says that he was Pinchas’s student as a commendation, as though the famous Pinchas ben Elazar were his teacher. But concerning Yochanan ben Narbai it says that he was Pankai’s student. Were this a commendation, the name of his teacher Pankai is not well known: who was he? If, however, he is Yochanan the high priest, who served eighty years in the high priesthood and then became a Sadducee, it makes sense that his teacher’s name was changed to his discredit, to Pankai: he was no longer Pinchas’s student. It also makes sense that, if the Yochanan here—Yochanan ben Narbai, Pankai’s student—was Yochanan the high priest, meaning the high priest who became a Sadducee and belonged to the Hasmonean house, he should have conducted himself with such grandeur and wealth, eating three hundred calves at his meal, with forty seahs of young birds as the final course, and drinking three hundred jars of wine: he was among the Hasmonean high priests and kings. There is a slight difficulty: why does it not count Mattityahu the high priest among the worthy priests? He was certainly a worthy high priest, mentioned in the Hanukkah miracle. This can be resolved; consider it carefully. End quotation. It requires examination in light of Yoma there: ‘Fear of God adds days’—the First Temple stood 410 years, and only eighteen high priests served in it; Ritva’s reading is twelve priests. ‘But the years of the wicked are shortened’—the Second Temple stood 420 years, and more than three hundred priests served in it. Subtract the forty served by Shimon the Righteous, the eighty served by Yochanan the high priest, the ten of Yishmael ben Pabi, and the eleven of Rabbi Elazar ben Charsom, totaling 141 years. Go and calculate: each of the others did not complete his year. This requires examination: why does it not count the eighty years served by Yochanan the high priest who became a Sadducee? One may answer that its ‘eighty served by Yochanan the high priest’ refers to the very man who became a Sadducee. But according to Beer Sheva, who writes in Maimonides’ name, Laws of Tithes, chapter 9, that there were two high priests named Yochanan: Rabbi Yochanan the high priest who abolished the tithe declaration lived after Shimon the Righteous, and was not the Yochanan the high priest who served eighty years and became a Sadducee. If there were two, one completely righteous and the other who became a Sadducee, why does it not count how long the righteous Yochanan the high priest served? Yuchasin writes that the Yochanan the high priest who served eighty years in the high priesthood and became a Sadducee was the son of Shimon son of Mattityahu; he was Hyrcanus the First and was called Yannai. Shalshelet HaKabbalah 25a, end, says that he served forty years in the high priesthood—a scribal error—and reigned thirty-one years.
